explanations.answer: Remember what has happened to them
explanations.explanation: The prayer opens with "Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us." Then it adds, "Look and see our disgrace!" (Lamentations 5:1). No warm-up, no small talk, just straight to Him. It's like a text that says "call me" and nothing else, friend.

explanations.answer: Punish Edom for all its sins
explanations.explanation: That isn't how this prayer starts. Its first words ask the LORD to "Remember" and to "Look and see." The prayer opens by bringing Him what has happened to them, and it doesn't open by naming anyone to punish.

explanations.answer: Send them a new king to lead
explanations.explanation: No king gets asked for in the opening line. The prayer says, "Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us." It wants Him to look at their disgrace first. I think they just need Him to see it before anything else.

That's what it says: "Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners." Inheritance means the land handed down in a family. Picture coming home and finding somebody else's name on the mailbox. Ouch.

The prayer says the opposite. "Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners." Their family land and their houses are in other hands now. That's the first item the prayer lays before the LORD.

Right, "We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price." Water AND wood, both with a price tag. Wood is what you burn to keep warm and cook. In my bakery, the oven's the one thing I never want to be short on.
Salt isn't in this line. The verse says, "We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price." So the second thing with a price is wood. I'll keep the salt out of it, friend.
Oil doesn't show up in this verse. It says, "We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price." Wood is the other thing that costs them. Even the basics have a bill attached.

That's the pair: "We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread." Egypt and Assyria were two other nations. Bread was the reason the prayer gives. When the pantry's thin, people will agree to a lot.
Close to a good guess, but those two names aren't in this verse. It says, "We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread." Egypt and Assyria are the two nations. Bread is the reason it gives.
Neither one is named in this line. The verse says, "We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread." So Egypt and Assyria are the two nations. Bread was what they were after.
Yes, "Our fathers sinned and are no more." It's a heavy line, and I won't pretend otherwise. The ones who sinned are gone now. The ones left are the ones talking to the LORD.
Yes, "but we bear their punishment." That's the second half of the heavy line, friend. The prayer says it plainly, with no dressing it up. They're carrying it, and they say so to the LORD.
The verse doesn't say enemies. It says "Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment." The ones who sinned are the fathers. The prayer is honest about that.

A blessing would be nice to inherit! But the verse says, "Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment." It's the punishment they bear, and it's a heavy line. The prayer says it out loud anyway.
Neighbors don't appear in this verse. It says, "Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment." The ones who sinned are the fathers. The prayer names them plainly.
Right, "Slaves rule over us." The prayer is describing how upside down things have gotten. Those who rule now are the ones you'd never expect. That's one more thing it hands to the LORD.
Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. It says, "Slaves rule over us; there is no one to deliver us from their hands." Slaves are the ones ruling. The prayer sets that out as part of the hurt.
Prophets don't come up in this line. The verse says, "Slaves rule over us." So slaves are the answer. It's a picture of a world turned over.
The prayer says the very opposite. "There is no one to deliver us from their hands." Nobody is on the way to rescue them in this verse. That's why the prayer turns to the LORD.
That's it, friend. The verse says, "there is no one to deliver us from their hands." Nobody is coming to rescue them in this line. It's a hard thing to say, and the prayer says it anyway.

Yes, "Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger." I know ovens, friend, and mine is hot on purpose, with cookies to show for it. Theirs is a fever, and the prayer says hunger is behind it. It's another heavy line, so I'll just say that once.
Wounds aren't named here. The verse says, "Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger." The fever comes from hunger. It's a heavy picture, and the prayer keeps it honest.
Weeping isn't what the verse says. It reads, "Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger." Hunger is the cause named. I think this one hurts to read.
The verse says the opposite: "elders receive no respect." Elders are the older leaders. So no respect is coming their way in this picture. The prayer says it honestly.

That's right. The prayer says "elders receive no respect." Elders, the older leaders, aren't getting any. It's one more piece of how things have turned over, and it goes right alongside "Princes have been hung up by their hands."
Yes, "Young men toil at millstones." A millstone is a heavy stone used for grinding grain. It's hard work, and I'd wobble just looking at it. The next line even gives the boys a load to carry.
Walls aren't in this verse. It says, "Young men toil at millstones; boys stagger under loads of wood." The young men are toiling at millstones. Grinding stones, not guard duty.
The temple isn't mentioned here. The verse says, "Young men toil at millstones." Millstones are heavy grinding stones. That's the work the young men are stuck with.

Yes, "Joy has left our hearts; our dancing has turned to mourning." Dancing is joy you can see, and here it's gone to mourning. I think that line is one of the saddest in the prayer. It takes the lively thing and flips it.
Anger isn't the word in this verse. It says, "Joy has left our hearts; our dancing has turned to mourning." The dancing turned into mourning. A sad flip, friend.
Fear isn't named here. The verse says, "our dancing has turned to mourning." Mourning is where the dancing ended up. It's one of the saddest lines in the prayer.
It does say it: "Woe to us, for we have sinned!" Earlier the prayer said, "Our fathers sinned and are no more" (Lamentations 5:7). Now "we" owns it too. It's honest, and it keeps right on praying.
The prayer says they have. "Woe to us, for we have sinned!" Earlier it said "Our fathers sinned and are no more" (Lamentations 5:7). Now the "we" speaks up for itself. Honest all the way through.

Yes, "Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes." Desolate means empty and left behind. Their eyes dim for it, and I think that's the heart of the grief. A place that was full is now just quiet.

No troops are mentioned in this verse. It says, "Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes." The word for it is desolate, which means empty, not crowded. Foxes are the ones walking around up there.

explanations.answer: It's been handed over to Edom
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. It says, "Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes." Desolate is the word. It's a place left empty, with only foxes on patrol.

explanations.answer: He reigns forever and His throne endures
explanations.explanation: Yes! "You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation." After all that loss, the prayer says this out loud. Everything else in the city fell apart, and here is something that stands. That's a big turn in the prayer, friend.

explanations.answer: He left His throne when the city fell
explanations.explanation: The prayer says no such thing. It says, "You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation." His throne endures. That's the turn right in the middle of all that loss.

explanations.answer: His throne now sits in a far country
explanations.explanation: That isn't in the prayer. The verse says, "You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation." It speaks of a throne that endures. Nothing here moves it anywhere.

It does. The very next line asks, "Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?" Those are the prayer's own words and its own question. It holds "You reign forever" and that aching question side by side, and it doesn't hide either one.

The prayer does ask it. Right after "You, O LORD, reign forever," it says, "Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?" That's the prayer's own question, spoken straight to the LORD. It keeps both in the same breath.
That's the one: "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return." They aren't asking first for a place. They're asking to be brought back to Him. A big ask indeed, and it comes from the heart.
Jerusalem isn't what this line asks for. It says, "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return." The one they want to be restored to is the LORD. It's the biggest ask in the whole prayer.
Their land isn't named here. The verse says, "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return." The prayer asks to be restored to Him. That's a bigger ask than any piece of ground.

The prayer actually ends the other way. The last line says, "…unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure." So a fear is still left on the table when the prayer stops. They set it before the LORD instead of hiding it.

Right. The last line says, "…unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure." The fear is still out in the open when the prayer ends. I think it's honest, and they bring it to the LORD instead of keeping it quiet.
